publications.name: The Newark Herald
publications.missionStatement: Dramatized the grievances and aspirations of African Americans in New Jersey, serving as a powerful voice for civil rights activities and political organizing in the Black community.
publications.historicalNotes: Published by the Newark Herald Publishing Co. as a weekly African American newspaper. Bibliographic description based on Vol. 11, no. 18 (June 11, 1938). The Herald's founder formed or helped form numerous political organizations including the Negro Progressive Republican League and the Young Men's Colored Republican Association of the City of Newark. Banner headlines addressed issues like 'Poor Housing Conditions are Assailed in Englewood' and 'Negro Must Use Politics to Win Rights.' Succeeded by the New Jersey Herald News (1938-1966). Historian Clement Price noted: 'Had not the black press in New Jersey dramatized the grievances and aspirations of the race, civil rights activities would have been without a powerful voice.' Available on microfilm at Newark Public Library and Rutgers Alexander Library. Newark Public Library has digitized issues in their African American Newark Newspapers collection. The Afro-American of July 9, 1932 reported from Newark that 'the Newark Herald, Jersey's only colored weekly, has ceased publication' after more than four years, that Editor Clark had left the Cotton Building, and that backers hoped to resume the paper (https://www.newspapers.com/image/1134167020/). The 1938 volume-11 issue suggests the title resumed or continued under the same count, so 1932 looks like an interruption rather than the final close.

publications.name: The Sentinel
publications.missionStatement: "Trenton’s first – and one of the state’s earliest – Black newspapers.”
publications.keyStaff: Founded, edited and published by R. Henri Herbert.
publications.historicalNotes: Founded by R. Henri Herbert, The Sentinel was Trenton's first and New Jersey's earliest African American newspaper. Herbert, born in 1857, began publishing the staunchly Republican weekly in his early twenties. Publication ran from Vol. I, no. 8 (June 26, 1880) through Vol. III, no. 19 (November 13, 1882). Herbert asserted the paper stood for 'earnest advocacy of the broadest freedom and purest liberty for white men, black men, Chinamen, and all men alike.' Advertisers included the Irish National Land & Industrial League, the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the local National Guard regiment, and the local Grand Army of the Republic chapter. The Sentinel later merged with the Trenton Herald at 4 North Broad Street. Herbert was a native of Trenton, son of Mansfield Herbert, a cabinet maker and artistic picture framer (whose clients included John A. Roebling). Henri's sister Priscilla Herbert was the first African American to graduate from the State Normal School (now College of New Jersey) in 1879. Issues were digitized from microfilm created by the Committee on Negro Studies of the American Council of Learned Societies and are available through Chronicling America. The New York Age of October 21, 1909 reported that Herbert died suddenly in Trenton and was found dead in the street; the Age identified him as a document clerk at the State House (https://www.newspapers.com/image/33451515/). A New-York Tribune profile of December 8, 1895 called him a noted colored leader of Mercer County and credited him with unifying Black Republican voters there (https://www.newspapers.com/image/78953914/). The Trenton Sunday Advertiser of November 5, 1893 printed 'R. Henri Herbert's Attack,' a letter asking his 'colored fellow-citizens' to help defeat Founder Bradley over the Asbury Park pavilion color bar (https://www.newspapers.com/image/1194114727/). The same paper on October 20, 1895 reported Herbert appointed a consulting member of the Republican State Committee (https://www.newspapers.com/image/1194116748/).

The publication sequence was: Black Newark (Vol. 1, Nos. 1-3, April-November 1968), then Black News (Vol. 1, No. 4, 1969, published by Black People of Newark), then Black New Ark (Vol. 1, No. 5, April 1972 through Vol. 2, No. 14, December 1973, published by CFUN), and finally Unity and Struggle (Vol. 3, No. 1, January/February 1974 through Vol. 8, No. 1/2, February 1979, published by CFUN as the national newspaper of the Congress of Afrikan People). These newspapers were published through the post-rebellion period of Newark, serving as tools for organizing and advocating for Black liberation and political and economic agency for Newark's majority Black citizenry. Baraka served as chairman of CFUN from 1968 to 1975. The movement documented in these papers contributed to the Black and Puerto Rican alliance that led to the election of Newark's first Black mayor, Kenneth Gibson, in 1970. The newspapers also covered Baraka's community-based initiatives addressing housing conditions, failing schools, and economic opportunities, including the Kawaida Towers apartment project and NJR-32 urban renewal project. The collection is digitized and searchable through the Rutgers Dana Library Newark Black Newspapers Collection. Additional copies are held at the NYU Tamiment Library and the Auburn Avenue Research Library. Scholarly treatment includes Jennifer Caroccio Maldonado's article 'Putting the Black Ink Back into Print: Black Newark/Black New Ark' in New Jersey Studies: An Interdisciplinary Journal 8(1), Winter 2022, pp. 34-49. Danky 1998 entry 934 spells the title Black New Ark; monthly; motto "The Voice of New Ark's Inner City"; variant Black News; WHi microfilm Apr-Nov 1968, Jan 1970, Apr 1972-Jan/Feb 1974. publications.historicalNotes: Founded in 1904 by William Elijah Rock in Long Branch, NJ. Rock was born at Pine Brook, NJ on January 22, 1861, son of Peter and Emma (Schanck) Rock, whose grandfather came from Africa and settled in New Jersey around 1700. Rock was educated in public schools at Pine Brook, received private instruction under Prof. John R. Porter in New York for 4 years, and read law in the office of T.W. Throckmorton in Red Bank for 8 years. The newspaper was named after his Lenni-Lenape mother Emma Schanck-Rock, per her original tribal name translated to English. Publishers listed as Rock and Howard. The Monmouth Democrat of September 8, 1904 reported that The Echo, 'a weekly negro newspaper published at Long Branch,' had been burned out, with suspected incendiary origin and several hundred dollars' damage to the press room; the first issue was edited by Rock & Howard (https://www.newspapers.com/image/497174278/). The Asbury Park Press of March 5, 1909 said Rock had edited The Echo in Long Branch for five years and had moved it to Red Bank, where he had bought a home (https://www.newspapers.com/image/143869436/). Relocated from Long Branch to Red Bank in 1909, established with capital of $50. Rock died in June 1933 and the paper folded in 1943. Was described as 'The oldest colored paper in New Jersey.' Per The State Historical Society of Wisconsin's Who's Who of the Colored Race Volume One (1915), Rock is listed alongside Madame C.J. Walker. Original issues available at Red Bank Public Library digital collection.

publications.historicalNotes: The New Jersey Afro-American was the Newark regional edition of the Baltimore-based Afro-American newspaper chain, one of the most influential African American newspaper enterprises in the United States. Published weekly by the Afro-American Company from Vol. 1, No. 1 (March 15, 1941) through 1991, it served the African American communities of Newark and East Orange in Essex County, New Jersey. The parent Afro-American newspaper was founded in 1892 by John H. Murphy Sr. in Baltimore and expanded under editor Carl J. Murphy (who led the paper for 45 years starting in 1922) to include nine national editions in 13 major cities. At its peak, regional weekly editions were published in Baltimore, Washington D.C., Philadelphia, Richmond, and Newark. The chain employed notable journalists and intellectuals including Langston Hughes, William Worthy, and J. Saunders Redding. It was the first Black newspaper to employ a female sportswriter (Lillian Johnson and Nell Dodson in the mid-1930s), and artist Romare Bearden began his career as a cartoonist there in 1936. During World War II, the Afro-American stationed reporters in Europe, the Aleutians, Africa, Japan, and other parts of the South Pacific; Elizabeth Murphy Phillips Moss was the first Black female war correspondent. The New Jersey edition adopted Afro-American numeration in 1979. Princeton University Library holds microfilm copies from March 15, 1941 through 1972. The parent Afro-American remains in publication today as the oldest family-owned African American newspaper in the United States. LCCN: sn84025926. A Daily Record story of May 21, 2023 reprinted a 1947 New Jersey Afro-American masthead (photo courtesy Jimmy Richardson) and stated that the New Jersey edition no longer exists (https://www.newspapers.com/image/962761544/). Courier-News 24 June 1991: Harry B. Webber started in the circulation department of the Afro American of Newark and later wrote the column Jersey Happenings for the Afro-American.

publications.name: New Jersey Trumpet
publications.missionStatement: Served the Black community in Jersey City and Newark during the late 19th century as a voice for African American interests in New Jersey.
publications.historicalNotes: A weekly newspaper published by Col. William H. Murrell (listed as 'Wm. Murrell'). First issue December 29, 1887; ceased around 1897. Originally based in Jersey City, it relocated to Newark in 1889. Murrell was born into slavery in Georgia and served during the Civil War as a valet to Confederate General Longstreet, later enlisting in the 44th regiment Virginia and South Carolina troops. After the war he moved to Louisiana, served in the State Legislature for nine years, and was a colonel of the 4th Regiment, Louisiana State National Guard. After losing his possessions in the great flood of 1878 and receiving death threats from the KKK, he moved to Washington D.C. (Treasury Department), then to New Jersey in 1883 where he established The Trumpet. His wife Louisiana served as business manager. Two of their sons, William Frederick and Wellington, were killed in the Spanish-American War and are buried in Arlington National Cemetery. Contemporary notices confirm the paper as a Black organ: the Evening World of December 11, 1888 reprinted an item 'From the New Jersey Trumpet—Negro Organ' (https://www.newspapers.com/image/50663302/). The Washington Bee of May 18, 1889 identified Col. William Murrell as editor of the New Jersey Trumpet when he received a new official commission (https://www.newspapers.com/image/46319440/). The Asbury Park Press of July 22, 1893 introduced 'Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet' as speaker on the colored question at a public meeting over beach and pavilion discrimination (https://www.newspapers.com/image/436760060/). The Shore Press of July 28, 1893 covered the same meeting and named him on the platform against James A. Bradley's pavilion signs (https://www.newspapers.com/image/436807841/).

evidence.caption: Colonel Murrell, editor of the New Jersey Trumpet, later James A. Bradley entered and was greeted with applause. The meeting was called to discuss the signs which James A. Bradley had posted on the pavilions forbidding their occupancy to the colored race.

publications.historicalNotes: CFUN News was the newsletter/newspaper of the Committee for Unified Newark (CFUN), the Black united front organization chaired by Amiri Baraka from 1968 to 1975. CFUN's primary publication was Black NewArk, first published in April 1968 as one of several media outlets Baraka developed to promote Black cultural nationalism. CFUN was formed after Ron Karenga and the US organization visited Baraka's Spirit House in Newark in 1967, driving a shift toward electoral organizing that led to the election of Newark's first Black mayor, Kenneth Gibson, in 1970. CFUN also operated a 'Black Newark' radio program on Newark Public Radio (c. 1970-72) where Baraka discussed topics from teachers' strikes to the origins of Kwanzaa. Digitized issues are in the Rutgers Dana Library Newark Black Newspapers Collection. Additional archival materials are in the Komozi Woodard Amiri Baraka Collection (Series IV, Box 3, Folder 6) at the Auburn Avenue Research Library, the Amiri Baraka Papers at Columbia University, and the George Washington University collection (1951-1988). The scholarly article 'Putting the Black Ink Back into Print: Black Newark/Black New Ark' by Jennifer Caroccio Maldonado (NJS: An Interdisciplinary Journal, Winter 2022) examines the publication's significance. publications.name: The Ironsides Echo
publications.keyStaff: Student editor (1932): Leon Snead; staff adviser (1940): Frances O. Grant; printing instructor: L. J. Roberts
publications.historicalNotes: Student newspaper of the Manual Training and Industrial School for Colored Youth at Bordentown (the 'Bordentown School'), also known as 'the Tuskegee of the North.' The school was founded in 1886 (originally 1876) by Rev. Walter A. Rice, a former slave and AME Church minister, beginning with 10 students in two wood-clapboard homes on West Street. The name 'Ironsides' derives from the school's location on the former estate of Commodore Charles Stewart, commander of the USS Constitution ('Old Ironsides') during the War of 1812. Frances O. Grant founded the drama club and The Ironsides Echo, which won multiple prizes from organizations including the National Scholastic Association. The paper was printed by students in the printing trades program and served as outreach -- both white and Black schools exchanged papers with them. The front page of the May-June 1939 edition announced Mary McLeod Bethune as Commencement Speaker. William R. Valentine became principal in 1915, viewing the school as offering practical education, stating: 'We cannot all be doctors, lawyers, dentists, and preachers... Thus the need of men in the trades.' The school closed in 1955 following the Brown v. Board of Education decision. Digitized issues (from 1935 onward) available through the New Jersey State Library's DSpace repository. publications.name: Black Women's United Front Newsletter
publications.primaryFocus: Women, Education, Prison reform, Economics, Book reviews
publications.historicalNotes: The Black Women's United Front (BWUF) was formally established on January 25, 1975, in Detroit, when over 500 activists from organizations including the Congress of African People (CAP), Youth Organization for Black Unity (YOBU), and the National Welfare Rights Organization came together. The BWUF was spearheaded by Amina Baraka (Sylvia Jones), wife of Amiri Baraka, who had led discussions about gender roles within CAP's Women's Division. Following the July 1974 All-Afrikan Women's Conference in Newark, NJ, Amina led over 800 men and women in forming the BWUF to develop 'an autonomous political and ideological agenda for African American women.' The organization committed to the 'abolition of every possibility of oppression & exploitation' and described itself as anti-racist, anti-capitalist, and anti-imperialist, rooted in working-class women. BWUF activities included political education forums, coalition building, support for the Joan Little case, and community forums on workplace rights, healthcare, and childcare. The BWUF published through Unity and Struggle rather than a standalone newsletter. Archival materials (1975-1976) are held in Series VII of the Komozi Woodard Amiri Baraka Collection at the Auburn Avenue Research Library on African American Culture and History, and are available on microfilm. Additional materials are accessible through the ProQuest History Vault (Penn Libraries) and the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Scholar Ashley Farmer's book 'Remaking Black Power: How Black Women Transformed an Era' draws extensively on these archives. The scholarly article 'Abolition of Every Possibility of Oppression: Black Women, Black Power, and the Black Women's United Front, 1970-1976' (Project MUSE) provides detailed analysis. publications.historicalNotes: Bronze Thrills was a Black romance and confessions-style magazine that evolved from The World's Messenger, founded in 1942 by Horace J. Blackwell, an African American minister and clothing merchant in Fort Worth, Texas. After Blackwell's death in 1949, his widow sold the publication to George T. Levitan, a white businessman, who renamed it Bronze Thrills and continued publishing through Good Publishing Company (also known as Sepia Publishing), based in Fort Worth. Bronze Thrills featured true romance, true confessions, and women's interest articles alongside essays on African American issues. While Sepia did not equal the newsstand sales of Bronze Thrills, it was Sepia that became the most successful competitor to Ebony for nearly four decades. After Levitan's death in 1976, the publications were sold to Beatrice Pringle, returning them to Black ownership. The business closed around 1983. Note: All available sources identify Fort Worth, Texas as the base of Good Publishing. The connection to Dover, New Jersey may reflect a regional editorial or distribution office, but this could not be confirmed through online sources. The magazine's records and building were mostly destroyed after the business closed; the African American Museum in Dallas now holds the picture files. publications.name: The Cricket: Black Music in Evolution

publications.missionStatement: The Cricket aimed 'to provide Black Music with a powerful historical and critical tool' and to enable avant-garde Black musicians and writers 'to finally make a way for themselves.' publications.keyStaff: Previous editor(s): Le Roi Jones, Amamu Baraka, Larry Neal, A. B. Spellman
publications.historicalNotes: The Cricket: Black Music in Evolution was edited by Amiri Baraka, A.B. Spellman, and Larry Neal between 1968 and 1969. Published by Baraka's Newark-based Jihad Productions, it was a mimeographed experimental music magazine that ran for four issues. The Cricket emerged from the heart of the Black Arts Movement, published shortly after the 1967 Newark Rebellion. Over its four issues, it laid out an anticommercial ideology and took aim at the conservative jazz press, providing space for critics, poets, journalists, and musicians to devise new styles of music writing. It ran poetry, position papers, and gossip alongside concert and record reviews and essays on music and politics. Contributors included Albert Ayler, Milford Graves, Sun Ra, Cecil Taylor, Stanley Crouch, Haki Madhubuti (Don L. Lee), Ishmael Reed, Sonia Sanchez, Keorapetse Kgositsile, Mtume, Black Unity Trio, Ben Caldwell, Askia Muhammad Toure, and many others. The fourth issue (1969) is particularly notable for containing Albert Ayler's letter 'To Mr. Jones -- I had a Vision,' describing an intense UFO sighting/religious revelation Ayler and his brother experienced in New Jersey. The complete facsimile of all four issues was republished by Blank Forms Editions with an introduction by poet and scholar David Grundy, author of 'A Black Arts Poetry Machine: Amiri Baraka and the Umbra Poets' (Bloomsbury Academic, 2019). publications.historicalNotes: Utimme Umana/La Voz Oculta was a minority student newspaper at Trenton State College (now The College of New Jersey). The original Utimme Umana was incorporated in 1968 as a Black student newspaper, though it initially struggled to gain footing. On October 2, 1972, the first issue of the combined Utimme Umana: La Voz Oculta was published, merging the Black student paper with a Hispanic voice. 'Utimme Umana' means 'rebirth' in Swahili, while 'La Voz Oculta' means 'the hidden voice' in Spanish. The paper's defining mission was to combat ignorance on the topics of race and it encouraged readers to help spread the word. The publication presented poetry, short stories, and essays relating predominantly to Black, Hispanic, and Latinx themes, along with social and cultural events, announcements, reviews, letters to the editor, photographs, and drawings. It was published twice monthly in newspaper format until early 1978 when it changed to a magazine format, with issues averaging 30 pages. The publication ran from 1972 to 1990. Its founding was part of a broader movement at Trenton State College where, following the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. in April 1968, African American students presented a list of 10 demands to President Robert Heussler, including creation of an Afro-American Studies program, increased Black student enrollment, hiring Black entertainment, and having a dedicated space on campus for Black students. Digitized issues are available through the TCNJ Digital Repository. Danky 1998 entry 6142: six times a year, Trenton State College, 28 pages. NCUP settled into the Clinton Hill neighborhood in South Newark in the summer of 1964, consisting of about 12-15 organizers (half Black, half white college students and graduates). While a specific newsletter titled 'NCUP News' was not confirmed in online sources, NCUP produced community publications and flyers as part of its organizing work in the predominantly Black Clinton Hill neighborhood. The project focused on housing issues, organizing rent strikes (which were illegal in New Jersey), picketing slumlords' homes, and conducting block meetings to address rats, roaches, unsafe living conditions, and police misconduct. NCUP's work is documented in the 1966 documentary film 'Troublemakers.' By late summer 1965, the project staff had dwindled to about half a dozen organizers, though an estimated 150 local people participated in various programs and meetings. The 1967 Newark Rebellion effectively ended NCUP, as the uprising convinced the remaining white organizers they were unwanted. NCUP's methods -- rent strikes, picketing, block meetings -- had by then spread to other parts of the city. Archival materials may exist at the NYU Tamiment Library, Rutgers University Libraries, or the Library of Congress, which catalogs materials under the subject heading 'Newark Community Union Project (N.J.)'. publications.historicalNotes: No digitized archive was found for Fire II from Trenton, NJ (1975). The title is a direct homage to Fire!! The original Fire!! lasted only one issue due to financial problems and a fire that destroyed remaining copies, but it became one of the most significant publications of the Harlem Renaissance for its unflinching treatment of Black life and its challenge to older Black literary conventions. publications.name: Unity and Struggle
publications.primaryFocus: Socialism, Black Liberation movement, Politics, Education, Employment, Housing, Health
publications.missionStatement: ‘The Struggle Continues”
publications.historicalNotes: Unity and Struggle was the national newspaper of the Congress of Afrikan People (CAP), led by Amiri Baraka. It evolved from earlier Newark Black publications: Black Newark (1968), Black News (1969), and Black New Ark (1972-1973), all published by the Committee for Unified Newark (CFUN). Unity and Struggle was issued by CAP from approximately February/March 1974 through April 1976, then by the Revolutionary Communist League (Marxist-Leninist-Mao Tse Tung Thought) from June 1976 through 1979, reflecting CAP's ideological transition from Black cultural nationalism to Marxism-Leninism. Dr. Komozi Woodard (professor of American history at Sarah Lawrence College and author of 'A Nation Within: Baraka and Black Power Politics') served as editor. The paper covered topics including African liberation, trade unions, factory organizing, and Black political conventions. The August 1974 issue featured coverage of the All-Afrikan Women's Conference held in Newark. The history of CAP was first published in Vol. V, No. 6 (June 1976). Digitized issues are available through the Rutgers Dana Library Newark Black Newspapers Collection (collections.libraries.rutgers.edu/newark-black-newspapers) and individual issues through RiseUp Newark (riseupnewark.com), with credit to the NYU Tamiment Library. Physical copies are held at the Komozi Woodard Amiri Baraka Collection at the Auburn Avenue Research Library, with a distribution list from 1975 preserved in the archive.

publications.historicalNotes: Right On! was the first original fan magazine catering to an African American teen audience, launched in October 1971 by the Laufer Publishing Company. Its first cover stars were The Jackson 5 (Michael, Jermaine, Tito, Jackie, and Marlon Jackson). The magazine was a companion to the white-audience teen magazines Tiger Beat and Bop. Cynthia Horner joined in 1976 as Editorial Director and shaped the magazine's identity for decades, becoming its most notable editor-in-chief. Right On! spawned spinoffs including Word Up! In the 1990s, the magazine passed through the Sterling/Macfadden publishing conglomerate (formed 1991-1992 when Macfadden's consumer magazines merged with Sterling's Magazines). In 1998, the youth music titles were sold to Primedia; the remaining titles were bought by Dorchester Media in 2004. Right On! ceased regular print publication in 2014. In 2017, Right On! Media Holdings, LLC was formed by Cynthia Horner (CEO), Derrick Horner (Chief Digital Officer), and Kenneth Harris (Chief Marketing Officer) to relaunch as Right On! Digital (rightondigital.com). The Cresskill, NJ listing may reflect a Bergen County office location, as the spinoff Word Up! was based in nearby Paramus, NJ. Some individual issues are available on Internet Archive. publications.primaryFocus: Labor, Trade unions, United Black Workers
publications.historicalNotes: The Black Voice was a Newark, NJ publication active from approximately 1972 to 1976, published by the United Black Workers, according to the Newark Public Library's inventory of New Jersey newspapers on microfilm. As a labor-affiliated Black publication, it served a distinct niche from the Baraka-era cultural nationalist newspapers (Black NewArk, Unity and Struggle) that were active in Newark during the same period. This should not be confused with the Black Voice News of Riverside, California (est. 1972), The Black Voice at Syracuse University (student publication, est. 1969), or the later Rutgers Black Voice Carta Latina (BVCL) student publication. publications.name: Word Up!
publications.historicalNotes: Word Up! debuted in August 1987 as a spin-off of Right On! magazine, headquartered in Paramus, NJ under Enoble Media and publisher John Blassingame. Rap Masters was its sister publication, both produced by Faces Magazines in Paramus. The magazine circulated from 1987-2012, proving indispensable in launching careers of countless hip-hop and R&B legends. In the 2020s, Cynthia Horner (former Right On! editor-in-chief) purchased both titles, forming Right On! Media Holdings, LLC. In 2023, the Notorious B.I.G. Estate partnered with Budweiser to release limited-edition tribute issues (5,000 copies each) during Hip-Hop 50 celebrations. publications.historicalNotes: Gospel Today was founded in 1989 by Dr. Teresa Hairston as a four-page newsletter, launched with just $300 while she was a divorced mother of three working two jobs. The newsletter grew into the longest-running and most widely distributed Urban Christian Lifestyle magazine in history. In 1992, Hairston launched companion publication SCOREBOARD (a gospel music industry trade journal), which later became Gospel Industry Today. Content expanded from gospel music coverage to all aspects of Christian lifestyle, featuring interviews with Denzel Washington, Whitney Houston, Evander Holyfield, Jesse Jackson, and others. At its peak, Gospel Today had a circulation of 240,000. In 2008, Lifeway Christian Bookstores pulled the magazine from shelves after it featured women pastors on its cover, conflicting with Southern Baptist beliefs. The magazine never fully recovered. Hairston stepped down in 2011, passing leadership to her son Roland T. Hairston II. The magazine transitioned to digital-only before ceasing operations circa 2013. Hairston also created the Gospel Today TV show (Word TV network) and founded the Gospel Heritage Foundation (1994). Her archival collection, including magazines, audio interviews, 5,000+ sound recordings, and promotional materials, was donated to Indiana University's Archives of African American Music and Culture (AAAMC) in 2016. Hairston published her memoir 'Unstoppable' in 2021. Danky 1998 entry 2656: bimonthly, published by Teresa E. Hairston, editor Kimberly Gilbert Crutcher. publications.name: Testimony: A Journal of African-American Poetry
publications.historicalNotes: Testimony: A Journal of African-American Poetry was a quarterly poetry journal published out of Montclair, NJ, edited by Sandra West. Two issues were published in 1987: Vol. 1, Issue One (Winter 1987) and Vol. 1, Issue Two (Spring 1987). Each issue was in 8.5x11 inch stapled wraps, running 30-34 pages. Issue One contained poetry on Black life, Black uplift, and Black alienation. Issue Two explored the political landscape with a pan-African scope, featuring poems including 'Apartheid,' 'Why Malcolm Had to Leave,' 'Frustrations of a NeoRevolutionary,' and 'Political FatCats.' Notable contributor Sonia Sanchez contributed 'MIA's (Missing in action and other atlantas).' The journal is extremely rare: only four institutional holdings are recorded in OCLC (Rutgers University, New York Public Library, Williams College, and Newark Public Library). No copies are known to be in commerce. The journal represents Montclair's role as a center of Black literary activity in northern New Jersey during the 1980s. publications.historicalNotes: This is NOT a newspaper. It is a digital library collection hosted by Rutgers University Libraries at collections.libraries.rutgers.edu/newark-black-newspapers. These newspapers served as tools for activism, organizing, and advocating for Black liberation and political and economic agency.
